content.comment_body: Hello, We are working on a refrigeration setup and want to use heating resistors for defrosting the evaporator. These resistors should be activated after a timer that tracks the operation time of the compressor or the magnetic shut-off valve. Both compressor and valve operate independently, with their own power supplies and temperature/pressure switches. Our goal is to track the actual time these devices are running. Once refrigeration stops and defrosting starts, the timer should reset and begin tracking again when refrigeration resumes. Defrosting should begin after a specific cumulative runtime, say 6–12 hours, and last for 20–40 minutes. During defrost, power to the magnetic valve must be cut, fans on the evaporator stopped, and heating resistors turned on. After the defrost cycle, everything should return to normal operation. I've included a diagram and picture for clarification. What is the recommended approach for monitoring the refrigeration cycle, accurately logging operational times, and triggering the defrosting process as described?

Additionally, the magnetic shut-off valve is a 24V AC model, while the PLC will likely be a 24V DC type. We don’t plan to directly supply power to the valve via the PLC—just use the PLC output to open or close the circuit. Is it possible to safely use the PLC output as a switch to control a phase powered by an external AC source?

Could you clarify your main question? 1. You could use a 24V AC [product_name] base module. Refer to the technical specs for different base modules. 2. To detect the temperature switch, connect it to an input (e.g., I1) if the voltage matches. Output Q1 can be managed alongside I1. 3. For measuring time, set up a counter with 1-second pulses when the condition is active. After 12 hours, the count should be 43,200, which you can check. 4. To heat for a set duration, use a relay block with timing. If you're unfamiliar with the basics of the [product_name] controller, programming it will be challenging. Please consult the online help of [product_name] software and the block descriptions available. Best regards, [user_name]

Understood. I've ordered the 24V DC version today. Two questions—here’s a summarized outline: Magnetic shut-off valve: Q1 acts as a switch in the valve circuit to break connection during defrost. Normally, Q1 is on. The valve itself is 24V AC, powered externally, and includes a temperature switch, solid state relay, and power supply. The PLC doesn't supply power to the valve but can override the external start/stop as needed for defrosting. Question: Is it safe to use Q1 simply as a switch for this AC line? Evaporator fans: Q2 used for switching four 24V DC fans. Heating resistors: Q3 switches two heating resistors (230 VAC, 800 W) via an external solid state relay. Tracking compressor operation: I1: Want to track compressor run-time to control cooling and trigger defrosting. Would using an additional solid state relay in parallel with the compressor to feed a signal to I1 work to indicate compressor activity?

I see what you mean with Q1. If no direct signal for defrosting is available as a controller input, your method works: pass the frosting signal via Q1 to the valve, and use a normal AC relay or suitable solid state relay in parallel with the valve to connect a contact to I1. When Q1 and I1 are both active, frosting is ongoing—use this for your counter or stopwatch. Operation hour counters measure full minutes only, so brief periods (under 60 seconds) aren’t counted, but standard counters have enough capacity for second-based tracking (up to 999,999). For all controller outputs, check technical specs for voltage/current limits. Use appropriate suppression devices depending on AC (varistor) or DC (diode). Best regards, [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: Participants discuss automating refrigeration defrost cycles by using a [product_name] PLC to track device operation time and control external components through relays. The main technical challenge is reliably monitoring the state and runtime of compressor and valve circuits, then using these signals to coordinate outputs for fans, heating resistors, and the magnetic valve. Practical advice is given regarding voltage matching, using solid state relays to isolate PLC from AC circuits, and leveraging timers/counters for accurate event timing.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect straightforward methods for voltage detection and device state monitoring, accurate runtime tracking, and dependable PLC-driven relay switching to automate defrost cycles in a safe and coordinated manner.
